  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Fast Food Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected, Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Vignette:
Samir Al-Fayed was thirty-nine when he stood on the corner of Elm and 4th at exactly 2:15 p.m., watching a delivery truck skid across wet asphalt and slam into a crowded bus stop. The impact sent a concussive blast of shattering glass and crumpling metal that echoed down the block. He had been walking back from lunch when the noise hit him first—a sharp, detonating crack that froze his blood. Paramedics and police swarmed the scene moments later, but what stayed with Samir was not just the wreckage; it was the shift supervisor who found him standing paralyzed on the sidewalk, gripping his keys like a weapon, and sharply corrected him for not moving faster or securing the area. The man’s clipped, impatient tone felt like another strike. Within days, Samir began pacing the exact 2:15 p.m. hour, convinced the pavement would still be warm. He stopped taking that route, then stopped taking the bus entirely. Over the following months, Samir’s world narrowed. He had come to believe that his apartment was the only place where the air felt still enough to breathe. Outside, every unexpected siren or dropped tool made his shoulders lock and his breath shallow; he was certain that a loud sound always preceded something unbearable. He stopped going out after dark, not because of the quiet, but because the silence felt like a holding pattern before another strike. When delivery drivers took too long to ring his doorbell, Samir would sit on the edge of his bed, fists tight, convinced the delay meant an accident had already happened. The waiting itself carried its own weight. Criticism or correction from strangers felt like it could unravel his composure just as easily as a blast, so he avoided grocery stores, construction zones, and crowded sidewalks. Now at forty-one, Samir works the afternoon shift at a fast-food franchise, a job he keeps because the predictable rhythm of grease hoods and ticket printers keeps his mind anchored. Yet the workplace is where his vigilance wears him down. He monitors the kitchen doors with the same wide-eyed scrutiny he once turned on street corners. When a fryer alarm blares or a manager calls him over to correct his plating procedure, his hands tremble, and he finds himself stepping back, waiting to see if the correction will spiral into something worse. The distance he puts between himself and the line has a visible cost: customers notice his hesitation, his speed drops, and his supervisor has begun leaving notes on his locker. Samir tells himself the notes are just paperwork, but the gap in his performance is widening, and the isolation of being single means there is no one at home to diffuse the tension before it pools in his chest. The turning point came three weeks ago when a power outage during the lunch rush plunged the kitchen into sudden silence, followed by the hum of backup generators. Samir had frozen at the register, unable to process the shift in sound, until a coworker tapped his shoulder. That moment, combined with a missed rent payment and a manager’s final warning, pushed him to book an intake. He sits in the waiting room now, eyes fixed on the door, wondering if the therapist’s office will be another place he cannot survive, or the first safe zone he has ever found. What frightened him most was that the noise of his own body would never quiet down, but what he quietly hoped for was a way to walk past 2:15 p.m. without bracing for impact.
